subtitle: How Songs and Sandals Wove a People Together

panels.shot: wide low-angle of Tukaram leading a distant, winding pilgrimage toward Pandharpur on the horizon
panels.action: Sant Tukaram stands at the edge of a dusty village path, cymbals raised, lips parted in song, as a long line of barefoot pilgrims stretches behind him toward the far-off temple town of Pandharpur shimmering in the heat.

dialogue.text: In the Maratha age, when forts rose and fell, Tukaram and the Warkari poets built another kingdom—of song and sandals—on the road to Pandharpur.

i18n.hi: मराठा ज़माने में, किलों की लड़ाइयों के बीच, तुकाराम और वारकरी कवियों ने पंढरपुर की राह पर गीत और पादुकाओं का एक अलग राज्य खड़ा किया।

panels.shot: broad aerial view over the Deccan plateau, with hills, forts and small river towns
panels.action: The camera soars above the parched yet patterned Deccan landscape, small fields and villages stitched between rocky hills, a fort perched on a distant ridge, while narrow roads snake toward riverbank towns.

dialogue.text: Seventeenth-century Maharashtra was a land of sieges and harvests, of new Maratha power and old village worlds, where temples and markets hugged the same rivers as marching armies.

i18n.hi: सत्रहवीं सदी का महाराष्ट्र घेराबंदी और फसल का, नई मराठा ताकत और पुरानी गाँव-गाँव की दुनिया का देश था, जहाँ मंदिर-बाज़ार और कूच करती फ़ौजें एक ही नदियों के किनारे बसते थे।

panels.shot: medium shot in Dehu village square
panels.action: In the small village of Dehu, Sant Tukaram sits cross-legged before a modest shrine, a rough stone Vitthal inside, while farmers, women with water pots, and children gather around, listening to him sing.

dialogue.text: In Dehu, near the Indrayani river, Tukaram of the grocer caste turned away from trade and war-talk, and turned instead to Vitthal, to rhythm, and to words that peasants and shopkeepers could taste.

i18n.hi: इंद्रायणी किनारे देहू में, किराना जाति के तुकाराम ने सौदागरी और जंग की बातें छोड़कर विठ्ठल को पकड़ा, ताल को पकड़ा, और ऐसी बोली पकड़ी जो किसान और बनिया दोनों चख सकें।

panels.shot: close-up on Tukaram's face as he sings, eyes half-closed
panels.action: Tukaram’s weathered face fills the frame, eyes half-closed in inward focus, mouth open mid-verse, small cymbals poised in his hands, with a faint outline of listening faces blurred behind him.

dialogue.text: He sang abhangas, short verses in village Marathi, carrying praise, complaint, and questions to Vitthal, drawing on an older river of saints—Dnyaneshwar, Namdev, Chokhamela, Eknath—who had praised the same dark god.

i18n.hi: वो गाँव की मराठी में छोटे-छोटे अभंग गाते, जिनमें स्तुति भी, शिकवा भी, सवाल भी, उसी विठ्ठल से; और पीछे बहती संतों की पुरानी धारा—ज्ञानेश्वर, नामदेव, चोखामेला, एकनाथ—सब उसी काले देव के गवैये।

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot from behind Tukaram facing the crowd
panels.action: From behind Tukaram’s shoulder, we see a small crowd of men and women in simple cotton, seated on the ground, some visibly from different castes, all focused intently on him as his hand moves in time to his unspoken song.

dialogue.speaker: sant_tukaram_and_the_warkari_poets
dialogue.text: Vitthal does not ask, ‘Of what birth are you?’ He asks, ‘How pure is your heart?’

i18n.hi: विठ्ठल नहीं पूछता, ‘कौन जात से है तू?’ वो पूछता, ‘दिल कितना साफ़ है तेरा?’

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot of earlier Warkari sites connected by the Indrayani river
panels.action: A flowing visual sequence links the riverbank at Alandi with Dnyaneshwar’s samadhi, a humble shrine at Paithan for Eknath, and simple village shrines along the Indrayani, all bathed in the same soft evening light.

dialogue.text: For centuries, the Warkari path had bound towns and castes—Dnyaneshwar at Alandi, Namdev of Pandharpur, Chokhamela the Mahar devotee, Eknath of Paithan—each leaving verses, tunes and a way of walking to God.

i18n.hi: सदियों से वारकरी की डोंगरी राह ने नगर और जात जोड़ रखी थी—आळंदी के ज्ञानेश्वर, पंढरपुर के नामदेव, महार भक्त चोखामेला, पैठण के एकनाथ—सबने ही भजन, धुन और भगवन तक की चाल छोड़ी थी।

panels.shot: medium shot of Tukaram at a low table with palm-leaf and paper manuscripts
panels.action: Tukaram sits in a dim interior, a low oil lamp casting light over palm-leaf and early paper manuscripts spread before him, as he writes with care, while a young boy watches in awe from the doorway.

dialogue.text: Tukaram’s songs did not stay on his tongue alone; scribes and disciples wrote them down on leaf and paper, a living Gatha that moved from palm to palm long before a printer in 1869 gave it fixed ink.

i18n.hi: तुकाराम के गीत अकेले उनकी ज़बान पर न रहे; शिष्य और लेखक उन्हें ताड़पत्र और कागज़ पर उतारते गए, एक ज़िंदा गाथा जो 1869 की छापाखाने की स्याही से बहुत पहले हथेली से हथेली चलती रही।

panels.shot: close-up of a hand copying verses onto worn manuscript leaves
panels.action: A calloused hand carefully copies Marathi lines onto a worn manuscript leaf, other leaves piled nearby, while in the blurred background villagers sit in a circle, mouths open in silent singing.

dialogue.text: Each copied page carried not just Tukaram’s words, but the pauses, tunes, and debates of those who recited them, so that every village added its breath to the text that later generations would call his.

i18n.hi: हर नकल की पन्नी में सिर्फ तुकाराम के शब्द नहीं, रुकावटें, धुनें, बहसें भी उतरती थीं, ताकि हर गाँव अपनी साँस उस लिखत में जोड़ दे, जिसे आगे चलकर लोग तुकाराम की कहेंगे।

panels.shot: wide shot of Dehu street where Brahmin and non-Brahmin listeners mix uneasily
panels.action: On a dusty Dehu lane, Tukaram sings at one end while a mixed crowd listens—upper-caste men in clean dhotis standing beside leather workers and laborers—some faces open, others frowning, a few turning away in disapproval.

dialogue.text: His abhangas cut against pride and ritual, mocking empty show and the arrogance of caste, so that some priests bristled, some landlords frowned, yet the poor and the quiet found their own tongue in his verses.

i18n.hi: उनके अभंग घमंड और खोखले कर्मकांड पर चलते, खाली दिखावे और जात-अहंकार का मज़ाक उड़ाते; कुछ पुरोहित झुँझलाए, ज़मींदार टीस गए, पर ग़रीब और चुप लोग उनकी पंक्तियों में अपनी ही ज़बान पा गए।

panels.shot: night-time wide shot of a simple house where a family repeats a remembered abhanga
panels.action: Inside a small lamplit hut, a family sits in a circle, an older woman leading a remembered tune while others follow, a child clapping softly, the mud walls close and warm around them.

dialogue.text: The songs walked from courtyard to courtyard, carried in memory, not by royal order; peasants repeated them at grindstone and well, making Tukaram’s sharp lines part of the way they scolded, comforted and hoped.

i18n.hi: ये गीत हुक्मनामा नहीं, यादाश्त के दम पर आँगन से आँगन चलते; किसान चक्की पर, कुएँ पर उन्हें दोहराते, और तुकाराम की तेज़ पंक्तियाँ उनके डाँटने, दिलासा देने, उम्मीद बाँधने के ढंग का हिस्सा बन गईं।

panels.shot: wide shot of early Warkari pilgrims gathering with small bundles and instruments
panels.action: At dawn near the Indrayani, a loose band of pilgrims assembles, some with simple cloth bundles, others with veenas and cymbals, their feet bare, faces set toward a direction beyond the frame.

dialogue.text: Around these songs grew practice: the Wari, the annual walk to Pandharpur, where people from Dehu, Alandi and beyond took the road together, village people turning the highway into a moving assembly.

i18n.hi: इन्हीं गीतों के आसपास अभ्यास पनपा—वारी, हर साल पंढरपुर की पदयात्रा, जहाँ देहू, आळंदी और दूर-दूर के गाँवों से लोग साथ सड़क पर उतरते, और गाँव वाले ही राजमार्ग को चलती जनसभा बना देते।

panels.shot: medium shot of Narayan Maharaj lifting a pair of wooden padukas
panels.action: A dignified Narayan Maharaj stands in a simple shrine, carefully lifting a pair of wooden padukas carved with care, while a handful of devotees bow and press their hands together in reverence.

dialogue.text: By the late seventeenth century, memory took a new form: Narayan Maharaj helped formalize the carrying of saints’ padukas, their wooden sandals, so that an absent guru could still ‘walk’ with the people to Pandharpur.

i18n.hi: सत्रहवीं सदी के आख़िर तक याद का नया रूप बना: नारायण महाराज ने संतों की पादुकाएँ—लकड़ी की खड़ाऊँ—उठाकर ले जाने की रीत जमाने में मदद की, ताकि ग़ैरहाज़िर गुरु भी लोगों के साथ पंढरपुर ‘चल’ सके।

panels.shot: long shot of a paduka palanquin leading a line of pilgrims along a dusty road
panels.action: The padukas, resting on a decorated wooden palanquin borne on the shoulders of devotees, sway gently at the head of a long line of pilgrims striding along a dusty road, fields and smoke from distant kitchens framing them.

dialogue.text: The palanquin of padukas became a moving shrine, its bearers chanting, its followers singing abhangas, so that the road itself was temple, and every halt became a shared court of justice and remembrance.

i18n.hi: पादुकाओं की पालखी चलती फिरती देव-मूर्ति बनी, कहार गान करते, पीछे वाले अभंग गाते; राह खुद मंदिर हो गई, और हर पड़ाव साझा न्याय और याद की खुली अदालत।

panels.shot: medium shot of Tukaram walking with pilgrims, singing while others join
panels.action: Tukaram walks in the midst of pilgrims, body lightly swaying, lips open in song, a farmer on one side and a woman laborer on the other, both matching his tune as the line of travelers stretches behind them.

dialogue.speaker: sant_tukaram_and_the_warkari_poets
dialogue.text: On this road we are one company; leave pride at home, carry only the Name.

i18n.hi: इस राह पर सब एक जत्था हैं; घमंड घर छोड़, साथ बस नाम ले।

panels.shot: wide shot of Warkari camp at night with shared meals and quiet singing
panels.action: At a riverside camp under stars, Warkaris sit in circles around simple meals laid on leaf plates, some sharing food across caste markers, others quietly singing as a small lamp flickers at the center.

dialogue.text: In the night camps of the Wari, hierarchy loosened and re-formed; though caste lines did not vanish, the shared march, shared food and shared songs taught villagers to imagine a fellowship wider than their hamlet.

i18n.hi: वारी के रात के डेरों में ऊँच-नीच ढीली भी पड़ी, नए ढंग से जुड़ी भी; जात की रेखाएँ मिटती नहीं, पर साझा चलना, साझा खाना, साझा गाना गाँववालों को अपने टोले से बड़ी संगत का एहसास सिखाता रहा।

panels.shot: low-angle wide shot of the pilgrims approaching the skyline of Pandharpur
panels.action: From a low angle near the dusty road, we see the mass of pilgrims cresting a rise, the skyline of Pandharpur ahead with its clustered rooftops and the unmistakable shikara of Vitthal’s temple breaking the sky.

dialogue.text: After days of heat and cracked feet, the dark tower of Vitthal’s temple rose before them, not as a distant royal monument, but as the end of a shared effort in which every step had been a prayer.

i18n.hi: कई दिन की धूप और फटी एड़ियों के बाद विठ्ठल के मंदिर का काला शिखर दिखता, किसी दूर के राज-मंदिर की तरह नहीं, बल्कि ऐसे मंज़िल की तरह, जहाँ हर क़दम पहले से ही प्रार्थना बना था।

panels.shot: overhead shot of the crowded Vitthal temple courtyard filled with Warkaris
panels.action: From above, the temple courtyard swarms with Warkaris, their white and saffron garments packed tight, hands raised, bodies swaying as their collective chant rises like a visible wave toward the inner sanctum.

dialogue.text: Inside Pandharpur, Vitthal’s stone form faced an ocean of faces, the temple priests still in charge of ritual, yet the words shaping the crowd’s mood were Tukaram’s, Namdev’s, Dnyaneshwar’s—a scripture sung, not proclaimed by decree.

i18n.hi: पंढरपुर के भीतर पत्थर का विठ्ठल चेहरों के समंदर की ओर, मंदिर के पुजारी अभी भी विधि के मालिक, पर भीड़ की रूह को गढ़ने वाले शब्द तुकाराम, नामदेव, ज्ञानेश्वर के—एक ऐसा शास्त्र जो गाया जाता, हुक्म से नहीं पढ़ा जाता।

panels.shot: close-up on a young pilgrim's face as he sings an abhanga with conviction
panels.action: A teenage pilgrim’s face fills the frame, eyes bright, mouth wide in full-throated song, a smear of dust on his cheek, as his voice joins unseen thousands around him.

dialogue.text: Through these abhangas, a ploughboy could say that God lived in the lowly, a maid could mock empty pomp, and both could measure king and landlord alike against a higher, sung measure of justice and humility.

i18n.hi: इन अभंगों के सहारे हलवाहा कह पाता कि भगवान नीच में बसते हैं, बाई ख़ाली तामझाम पर हँस पाती, और दोनों ही राजा-ज़मींदार को किसी ऊँचे, गाए हुए तराज़ू से तौल पाते—इंसाफ़ और विनम्रता के।

panels.shot: time-lapse style montage of years turning as Wari processions continue
panels.action: A stylized sequence shows Wari processions in changing details—older turbans giving way to newer dress, lanterns to hurricane lamps—yet the same paduka palanquins and lines of singing pilgrims continue across the years.

dialogue.text: Empires shifted—from Adil Shahis to Mughals, from Maratha confederates to British rule—but the Wari and the abhangas remained, adapting yet steady, a yearly rehearsal of a community that rulers could not fully script.

i18n.hi: साम्राज्य बदलते रहे—अदिलशाही से मुग़ल, मराठा सरदारों से अंग्रेज़ राज तक—पर वारी और अभंग बने रहे, बदलते भी, टिके भी, हर साल ऐसी सभा का अभ्यास जो हाकिम भी पूरी तरह लिख नहीं सके।

panels.shot: modern-era wide shot with contemporary Warkaris on the road, Tukaram's image on a small banner
panels.action: On a paved modern road, present-day Warkaris in simple yet contemporary dress walk barefoot, some carrying a small banner with Tukaram’s likeness and verses, while buses and power lines stand quietly in the distance.

dialogue.text: Today, Tukaram’s Gatha lives in printed books, recordings and loudspeakers, yet still most deeply on the Wari road, where his songs and those of fellow saints offer a moral language that outlasts edicts, flags and courtroom speeches.

i18n.hi: आज तुकाराम की गाथा छपी किताबों, रिकॉर्डिंग और लाउडस्पीकरों में है, पर सबसे गहराई से अभी भी वारी की राह पर, जहाँ उनके और दूसरे संतों के गीत हुक्म, झंडे और अदालत की लंबी दलीलों से ज़्यादा टिकाऊ नैतिक भाषा देते हैं।

title_i18n.hi: तुकाराम के गीत पंढरपुर तक चलते हैं

subtitle_i18n.en: How Songs and Sandals Wove a People Together
subtitle_i18n.hi: गीतों और पादुकाओं ने कैसे लोगों को जोड़ा
